content: Apamin is a neurotoxin that specifically inhibits SK channels, which are small-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels found in the central nervous system. This polypeptide, composed of 18 amino acids, is a component of bee venom (apitoxin). It is primarily utilized in biomedical research to investigate the electrical properties of SK channels and their involvement in afterhyperpolarizations, which occur immediately after an action potential in neurons. Apamin was originally isolated from the venom of the Western honeybee, Apis mellifera. Honeybee venom is a complex mixture containing various bioactive components, including melittin, the MCD peptide, and phospholipase A2, in addition to apamin. Chemically, apamin is a polypeptide with the amino acid sequence COOH-Cys-Asn-Cys-Lys-Ala-Pro-Glu-Thr-Ala-Leu-Cys-Ala-Arg-Arg-Cys-Gln-Gln-His-NH2. It contains two disulfide bonds, specifically between Cys1-Cys11 and Cys3-Cys15. Due to the complexity of honeybee venom, isolating apamin is challenging and requires techniques such as electrophoresis or chromatography. Pharmacologically, apamin binds to SK channels in the brain and spinal cord, inhibiting their function. It blocks the three known SK channel subtypes (SK1, SK2, and SK3) with varying affinities: it has the highest affinity for SK2, the lowest for SK1, and an intermediate affinity for SK3. Heteromeric SK channels exhibit intermediate sensitivity to apamin. The mechanism of action likely involves apamin acting as a pore blocker, although residues both within and outside the pore region of SK channels contribute to its binding. SK channels are widely distributed in both excitable and non-excitable cells, including neurons, intestinal smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells, and hepatocytes. When activated, SK channels mediate afterhyperpolarizations in neurons, which regulate neuronal excitability. These channels are activated by intracellular calcium binding to calmodulin, and they deactivate when calcium dissociates from calmodulin. By inhibiting SK channels, apamin increases neuronal excitability and lowers the threshold for action potential generation. Other toxins, such as tamapin and scyllatoxin, also block SK channels. The toxicity of apamin, as part of bee venom, can manifest in various symptoms. Local effects include burning or stinging pain, swelling, and redness. Severe systemic reactions may involve swelling of the tongue and throat, difficulty breathing, and anaphylactic shock. Other potential complications include optic neuritis and atrophy, atrial fibrillation, cerebral infarction, acute myocardial infarction, Fisher's syndrome, acute inflammatory polyradiculopathy (Guillain-Barré syndrome), and claw hand. The latter is caused by a combination of central effects of apamin on the spinal cord and peripheral effects, such as median and ulnar neuritis, leading to spasms of the forearm flexor muscles. Additionally, apamin can cause a dramatic hemorrhagic effect in the lungs. Treatment for bee venom poisoning includes the administration of anti-inflammatory medications, antihistamines, and oral prednisolone. Therapeutically, SK channel blockers like apamin have potential applications in both peripheral and central systems. For instance, they may influence insulin-releasing cells in the pancreas. In the central nervous system, SK channels are implicated in memory processes, particularly in the hippocampus. Consequently, SK channels have been proposed as therapeutic targets for conditions such as ataxia, epilepsy, memory disorders, and potentially schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.
